query: CDW's revenue recognition: criteria for hardware vs. software vs. services.
final_answer: ### Hardware - **Principal vs. agent:** CDW acts as a **principal** for hardware sales, so revenue is recognized **gross** (sales price in Net sales; acquisition cost in Cost of sales). - **When revenue is recognized:** When **control passes to the customer**, usually **upon delivery**, typically based on the **shipping terms** in the customer contract. - **Drop-shipments:** Even when hardware is **drop-shipped** directly from vendors to customers, CDW is still the **principal** and recognizes revenue **gross**. - **Bill-and-hold:** If a customer requests delayed delivery, control is deemed to pass when the hardware is **ready for delivery**, which CDW assesses using factors including: signed agreement, transfer of significant risks/rewards, customer ability to direct use, item set aside and not redirectable, and (if applicable) configuration services completed. - **Warranties:** Manufacturer (OEM) warranties are **assurance-type** and **not separate performance obligations**. Separately sold **extended warranties** are treated as **separate performance obligations** (addressed under services). ### Software - **What it includes:** Software revenue includes **perpetual licenses, term licenses, software assurance, and cloud computing solutions**. - **Principal vs. agent depends on arrangement:** CDW may be **principal or agent** depending on the nature of the software transaction. - **Enterprise agreements (EAs) / software assurance under EAs:** For most EA transactions, CDW’s role is typically a **distributor/sales agent** where the vendor provides the services/licenses and may invoice the customer directly; CDW’s performance obligation is satisfied **at the time of sale**. CDW records the **agency fee/commission in Net sales** with **no corresponding Cost of sales** (net presentation). ### Services - **What it includes:** Services include **professional services**, **hosted and managed services**, and **vendor partner delivered services**. Recognition depends on whether CDW is principal or agent: - **Professional services (principal; gross):** Recognized **gross** either (a) **time-and-materials** for variable contracts, or (b) for fixed-fee contracts, recognized **proportionally as costs are incurred relative to total estimated costs** (input method). - **Hosted and managed services (principal; gross):** Generally **stand-ready obligations**; recognized **gross, ratably over the contractual term**. - **Vendor partner delivered services (agent; net):** CDW arranges for the vendor to provide the service (example: **extended warranties**); revenue recognized **net at the point of sale**.

query: Impact of Church & Dwight coupon reserve mthd on P&L & cash flow w/ redemp variances: CHD
final_answer: Church & Dwight’s coupon reserve methodology affects the **P&L (net sales)** through **variable consideration/promotional reserves**, and affects **cash flow** mainly through the **timing difference** between when the reserve is recognized vs. when coupons are actually redeemed/paid. ## P&L impact (including redemption variances) - CHD treats consumer coupons as **promotional reserves** and **nets all such costs against sales (revenue)** rather than recording them as an operating expense. Coupon-related discounts are **recorded when the related sale takes place** (i.e., when the product sale that generates the coupon obligation occurs). - The coupon reserve is estimated using **historical experience** (e.g., projected coupon redemption rates) and forecasted data. - Sensitivity disclosed: based on recent years’ coupon activity, if **actual coupon redemptions deviate by 0.1%** from the redemption rate used to accrue reserves, the required coupon reserve would differ by approximately **$0.7 million**. This would flow through the P&L as a change in **net sales** (because coupon costs are netted against sales). ## Cash flow impact (including redemption variances) - Because CHD accrues coupon costs at the time of sale, but **cash is paid later when coupons are redeemed**, the reserve creates a **working-capital timing difference**: - If **actual redemptions are higher than estimated**, CHD would need to **increase the reserve** (reducing net sales) and would also generally see **higher cash outflows when redemptions are paid**, with the cash impact showing up through changes in accrued liabilities/working capital in operating cash flow. - If **actual redemptions are lower than estimated**, CHD would **reduce the reserve** (increasing net sales) and would generally have **lower subsequent cash outflows**, again reflected through working-capital changes. In short: redemption-rate variance primarily drives **net sales volatility** via reserve true-ups (e.g., ~**$0.7 million** per 0.1% redemption-rate change), while cash flow is impacted by **when** the redemptions are paid relative to when the reserve is recorded.
